speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: FIRST AND SECOND READINGS OF PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext:
I rise to a point of order.
Standing order 116 states:
Except in eases of urgent and pressing necessity, no motion for the suspension or modification of any standing order applying to private bills or petitions for private bills shall be entertained by the house until after reference is made to the committee on standing orders or to one of the committees charged with the consideration of private bills, and a report made thereon by one of such committees.
I submit that under this standing order the motion is out of order.

subtopic: FIRST AND SECOND READINGS OF PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext:
Under ordinary circumstances I should say that the point was well taken; but, the hon. member must read carefully the first line of standing order 116 from which he has just quoted:
Except in eases of urgent and pressing necessity.
The raison d'etre of the present motion is that the session will soon conclude, and if these bills are to be entertained by the house, standing order 105 must be suspended. Notice was given of this motion, and in my judgment, reading standing order 116 as it should be read,
I rule the motion in order. Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The object
of this amendment to the Yukon Quartz Mining Act is to assist in the better administration of the act and to prevent action being taken by claim jumpers where very substantial compliance with the regulations has been undertaken by the lessee. One case arose in the Yukon over the fact that the location was not quite accurately described, and there was some slight difficulty with regard to payment. Another action is about to be commenced dealing largely with the size of the stakes, and this amendment is designed as a direction to the court that where substantial compliance with the regulations has been undertaken and carried out, the full and minute compliance with the regulations as provided in the act will not entitle the court to give a decision cancelling the lease.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Life-saving service, including rewards for saving life, $80,000.
Would the minister advise the committee of his intention as to placing a lifesaving station at Scatarie island?

speakeroldname: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I realize the importance of the matter which was raised by my hon. friend last night, but I doubt very much if he appreciates the extent of the expenditure necessary were the government to accede to all the representations which are made in regard to the establishment of live-saving stations. The government last year considered the matter of placing a life-saving station at Scatarie island, and it also considered the placing of similar stations at Whitehead and Halifax. When the matter of costs was looked into it was found that it would cost $550,000 to set up these three stations with modern life-saving equipment. The committee will realize what it would cost if this service were extended all over the country. I must confess that when my officers submitted that figure I was somewhat frightened, and I hesitated to ask parliament to vote such a large sum for the establishment of these life-saving stations. The department is not losing sight of the importance of such stations at certain points, but we must realize that it would be impossible for Canada to meet all the requests which have been made for the establishment of life-saving stations. During the last session hon. members from Toronto complained because the department had not established sufficient life-saving stations on the great lakes and that we were not fulfilling our duty in protecting life on these inland waters. If we were to establish modern life-saving stations all over the country it would cost millions of dollars. The United States has been cited as an example, but I visited one of their life-saving stations last year and as far as efficiency is concerned I do not thinlc they are very much ahead of Canada. In that .country the life-saving organization is joined with the coast guard service and Canada might consider the joining of our life-saving service with the protective and patrol service of the National Revenue department and the Fisheries department. I was told by the man in charge of this station which I visited that he had been there for twenty-five years and during that time he had not used the devices which were placed at his disposal. A small gasoline boat on the great lakes would be of very little assistance to a vessel which might be in difficulties in the middle of the lake or at the opposite end, and to give effective service it would mean

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
the establishing of a very expensive organization, and I think we should hesitate before entering into such a large program.
The case of Scaterie island is still being considered by the department. At the present time the deputy minister is in England investigating the system which they have there, and I would advise the hon. member for Richmond-West Cape Breton (Mr. Macdonald) that the case of Scaterie island is very well known to the deputy minister. After giving this matter very careful and full consideration I came to the conclusion that if these requests are to be met it will be necessary for me to come before parliament and ascertain if it is the desire of the house that we have a yearly expenditure of over $1,000,000. The amount for which we are asking is not very large, $80,000, when one considers the extended service which is provided. Our Object always has been to meet the conditions which arise at particular points which we consider to be the most important as far as protecting life is concerned. I realize that Scatarie island is an important point and I can assure my hon. friend that that matter is not being lost sight of.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has made reference to the great lakes and to the city of Toronto, and before this vote is passed I would like to refer to the complaints which have been made as to the inspection service of passenger boats on the great lakes and the inadequate supply of rafts and lifesaving apparatus on those boats. Some of the boats are from twenty to thirty years old and they are still carrying very heavy passenger lists across the great lakes. Perhaps the minister would make a few observations with regard to this particular inspection service over which he has control and as to the adequacy of the life-saving apparatus on these vessels.

What my hon. friend has mentioned was the subject of certain study, but one of the hon. members representing the city of Toronto made a direct observation with regard to the life-saving stations that we have around the lakes. With regard to the last point raised by my hon. friend, this is the business of the ship inspectors, and the instructions which they receive from the department are very strict. If my hon. friend has any case in which the inspector has not been fulfilling his duty, I shall be glad to hear of it and to take the necessary means to correct it.

I took some part in that
discussion last year when one of the Toronto 
members brought up the matter. I suggested at the time that the department or the government should have some form of meeting with the vessel owners and the employees on the boats in order to discuss the question of curtailing the movements of vessels to a certain extent for the last few days at least of the season's navigation. My recollection is that the minister at that time said that such a proposal wras intended to be carried out. What has been done in that regard?

We have always made representations to the ship owners to cease navigating the lakes when the season was reasonably closed. We find that most of the accidents happening on the lakes occur after what we call the regular or reasonable close of navigation. But we have always been making representations to these companies that they should not take upon themselves the great risk of navigating the lakes when the reasonable season is closed. They are not always disposed to act upon the representations we make. We are trying to curtail as much as possible the risks they are taking in navigating too late on the lakes.

I entirely agree with the minister that the danger is after the reasonable season of navigation is over. At times an attitude of carelessness has been taken towards the lives of the men employed upon vessels. I wish again to impress upon the minister the reasonableness of endeavouring to have what has been suggested carried out. I do not wish to suggest an unreasonable curtailment of the season of navigation, but certainly it should be the duty of parliament as far as possible to preserve the lives of the seamen from any absolutely unnecessary dangers to which they are exposed by an unreasonable extension of the navigation period.

I note that the minister objects to improvement of the life-saving station at Scatarie island, and I am very sorry that he takes this attitude. He claims that if we are going to establish one station we should have two or three. Anybody acquainted with conditions on the Atlantic coast realizes the dangers to which shipping is exposed and I am sure that if the minister and the deputy minister had taken the interest in this matter that they should have taken in the past, they also would be cognizant of the situation at Scatarie island and would have taken steps to provide the remedy. The cost of giving them at least some form of life-saving station would not amount to more than $25,000, and I claim that Scatarie island is second only to Sable

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
island in being the most dangerous point on the north Atlantic coast. During the last five years there has not been a year without at least twenty-five or thirty lives having been exposed on that coast. Last year thirty lives were lost off that very island and the previous year five lives were lost. During the last five years not one year has passed without four or five lives being lost. These men were not all Canadians, it is true, but if the government takes the attitude it does, I cannot see how we are going to relieve the existing situation. We spend enormous sums of money for other things, but we cannot find a dollar to spend for the saving of human life. Would it not be better for the department and the deputy minister to take the money they are now spending in other directions and utilize it for the establishment of a proper life-saving station at Scatarie island? It is my intention to bring this matter up on every occasion and I am going to press for it because I consider it essential in the interest of the country. It is one of the most humane things we can do. The poor sailor who goes out to sea is risking his life at all times, and it should be our duty to furnish him with every possible safeguard and to do everything we can to minimize the risks of his hazardous calling.

I wish to join with the hon. member for Richmond-West Cape Breton in impressing upon the minister the necessity of some improvement in the life-saving service at Scatarie island. It does not form part of my constituency, but it is perhaps the most dangerous point on the Atlantic coast and the equipment there now is totally inadequate. It would not cost anything like a million dollars to equip the station properly. If the minister secured a vote of $10,000 or $15,000 for a proper boat there, that would fulfil the requirements at the present time, but something is urgently needed at that point.

Has any provision
been made for life-saving at Sable island?
I am informed there is a life-saving station there.
If Sable island has a life-saving station, there is certainly every necessity for one at Scatarie island.
There is also one at Scatarie island. The complaint is that it is not big enough.

I think Scatarie island, more than any other island on the Atlantic coast with perhaps the exception of 78594-211
Sable island, is entitled to a life-saving station. I certainly agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Richmond-West Cape Breton that the government should do something at once to provide means there of protecting the lives of the sailors. The sum need not necessarily be a large one. Disasters of all kinds are happening every year and have been happening for many years around that island.

The
minister said there was a life-saving station at Scatarie island. If he calls the present equipment that the government has placed on Scatarie island a life-saving station, it is a disgrace to the government and the country. Scatarie island is in my constituency and I have visited it on more than one occasion. The island is situated nine miles from the mainland of Main a Dieu and I would not for a minute go into a pool the size of this parliament building in the lifeboat that is now at Scatarie island. You can see daylight through the bottom of the lifeboat. We have no life-saving crew on Scatarie island. The government supplied a boat there some years ago and that is as far as the government has gone in that regard. The only time the lifeboat was ever used- was when volunteers went out in it and the government pays them the paltry sum of a dollar or two when they go out. I do not believe there is a man on the island who would risk his life by going out in that boat. It is up to the government to give the matter some consideration. The minister cannot understand the seriousness of the situation when he stands up in this house and makes the statements he does. It would pay the minister if he or his deputy or one of his officials were to visit that spot and see the wrecks that are strewn around that coast, and let him ask any of the men in the vicinity as to the number of human lives that have been lost there in the last five years. If the minister would only look into the situation, I am sure he would not make the statements he does.

I wonder if the minister has ever been down by the Atlantic ocean when there was a storm. I recall being on the Atlantic coast when one of those fierce storms came in from the sea, and when you observe what takes place around any of these small islands, and especially if there happens to be a fog, as there frequently is-well, I should not like to be the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and feel that I had not utilized the public exchequer to provide facilities there for life-saving. I say that to the minister very seriously. I travelled along that coast last



Supply-Marine and Fisheries
year by motor. Part of the time it was very foggy, and once there was a very heavy storm. There are wrecks of ships along that Nova Scotia shore and skeletons are sometimes washed up of men who have lost their lives. Seatarie island has been responsible for the loss of a good many vessels and many lives, and I suggest to the minister that he could provide at least reasonably decent life-saving facilities out of the miscellaneous vote. To carry into effect the suggestions that have been made would not cost I should think more than S2,500 at the moment. I think you could get a lifeboat and small station with that much money, or with $5,000, say, you could provide a gun and a decent boat. I made some inquiries about what these things cost; I am only speaking from memory that is now eight or ten months old, but I think $5,000 would defray the cost of a gun and a decent lifeboat. Now I put this to the minister: Can he rest quietly with the thought that we are voting $100,000 for advertising, $150,000 to do this and $50,000 for something else, when for $5,000 he could provide facilities which might save the lives of half a dozen people, or even only one life? I cannot think that Canada is doing its duty in leaving that island in its present condition, and I do press the minister to say now that he will provide these lifesaving facilities out of the miscellaneous vote. I am sure that the Prime Minister would not baulk at a governor general's warrant, if it became necessary, to provide a few thousand doHars for a cause such as that. I do press the minister not to leave this over for another year. I remember the head of a great shipping corporation telling me that when there were storms and his ships were passing along a certain dangerous shore, he could not sleep at night. That was before the days of wireless. Here we have that condition intensified, and I do press the minister to provide these life-saving facilities.
The hon. leader of the opposition may rest assured that we are not losing sight of the importance of the service that has been suggested.
But you have.

The lives which have been lost in that vicinity are not due to the lack of what may be called proper life-saving appliances. They are due to accidents which the ships have met with, and nobody can contend that the lives that were lost would have been saved if instead of having one life boat we had two or three.
But you cannot call this a boat at all. It is useless; it is unsafe.

It is used once in a while
at all events.

That
boat has not been in the water for years. It is there for ornament.

Apparently the boat has
not been needed. I would not like to be taken as minimizing the importance of the lifesaving service. I quite agree with the hon. member for Richmond-West Cape Breton and the hon. leader of the opposition that it is important to have life-saving facilities even if they are not used, because of the greater confidence and the greater sense of security they give to navigators and the crews of vessels. They feel that there is something there to take care of them if an accident does come.

You certainly could buy
a gun to shoot a line across to a ship.
There is one there already.
It is no good, I am told.

Certainly it is good, but
I have no objection to meeting the reasonable request that has been made by the hon. gentlemen, and I will see if I cannot take something out of the general vote to meet the situation.

The
minister states that there is a gun on the island. Where is it placed, and when was it placed there?
I am informed that the gun was placed' there in 1927.
After the wreck of 1926.
Yes.

After I
had brought the matter to the attention of the house. What class of gun is it?
It is a line throwing gun.

How
large?
It is the standard size.

For the benefit of the minister I may say that the gun that is on the island is of absolutely no use to the people on the island. This is a fishing community, with twenty-five families living on the island, and they have no roads over which they can transport the gun which the government has supplied. That just shows the information which the government has as to conditions there. They have a gun that cannot even be transported from one

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
place to another. The government should send someone to that island to make an inspection and see just what is necessary. The minister says that no lives were lost as a result of there not being proper life-saving devices. I tell him that five lives were lost in 1926 as a* result of not having the equipment to fire a line aboard a ship. The captain of that ship told me personally-I was with him for five or six days both on Scatarie island and in the town of Louisburg-he waited all night for a line to be fired aboard his ship, and all the time his ship was breaking up and the timber was going mountains high, huge timbers were being crushed to splinters, while he and his orew of thirty men watched the fires burning which the fishermen had lighted on the shore. Those five human lives could have been saved if there had been equipment on the island to fire a line aboard that ship, and I say it is up to this government to look into this situation and provide these life-saving facilities. The facilities could have been used every year in the last five years if they had been there, but there are not proper facilities on the island at the present time. What is there is wholly inadequate.

Item agreed to.
Hydrographic and tidal and current surveys, and to provide for the maintenance and repair of hydrographic steamers, $495,000.
How many vessels are engaged in the hydrographic service at the present time and where are they stationed?

On the Pacific coast we
have the steamer Lillooet and the auxiliary house boat the Somass. On the Atlantic coast we have the Acadia, the Cartier and the Bayfield.

Have you any engaged in
the Hudson bay?

The Acadia is going up
there this summer.

Have you any on the great
inland lakes?
We have none.
I notice in the supplementary estimates there is a vote of $400,000 for a new hydrographic survey boat. Is that right?
Yes.

On what pant of the coast
will that boat be put in service?

It is for general work on
the Pacific coast.

We find along the British
Columbia coast-and I refer now particularly 78594-211i
to the waters north of Vancouver and extending along the whole of Hecate strait, including the Queen Charlotte waters-that there is the greatest need for hydrographic survey work. Let me give an illustration of the hopeless lack of these surveys. A few weeks ago a large company engaged in very extensive logging operations on the Queen Charlotte islands entered into a contract with a transportation company to take out some million logs. The contract contained a clause which had been overlooked by one of the parties; it was to the effect that before the vessel would go into Moore channel the survey chart would have to be produced. There Was no survey chart for this channel. Telegrams were sent to Ottawa, and I took the matter up with the Department of National Revenue, thinking it came under that department. Then I went down to the hydrographic branch and found that the admiralty charts which were supposed to cover these waters had not been printed for years; in fact they are practically out of print and useless. This is the telegram that I received:
On account of extensive activities now going on west coast of Queen Charlotte islands the Queen Charlotte City board of trade request you immediately to take up matter of surveying Moore channel by steamer Lillooet to check up and supplement chart number two one six eight.
It was impossible for the Lillooet to be put on this survey work. The man concerned, had he failed to take out the logs, would have lost thousands of dollars. Therefore he had to go down to San Francisco and buy a steamer to carry out his contract.
At this moment I am not blaming anybody, directly, but I do wish to bring this home to the minister. The Lillooet, an eight hundred ton boat is not fitted to go out into the rough waters contiguous to the Queen Charlotte islands ; in a word, she is not capable of doing the hydrographic survey work along that coast. We are sadly lacking in up-to-date hydrographic survey boats capable of carrying on the work in those dangerous waters. I would impress upon the minister the urgent necessity of setting aside a boat exclusively for this work of charting the waters of the Hecate strait and the adjacent waters. Since the Lillooet cannot be spared from the Vancouver coast, I would recommend to the minister that now 'he is organizing and extending this very important survey work he should take steps to place a suitable hydrographic survey boat in these waters and keep her there for the next seven years on intensive hydrographic survey work.

It is precisely because we
realize the importanace of what my hon.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
friend has referred to that in the supplementary estimates we are providing for a new boat.

Mr. Chairman, the member
for Skeena does not tell the house that the hydrographic survey boat has been operating off the Queen Charlotte islands for years and years, to the neglect of the interests lower down the coast, and if the boat has been transferred to Vancouver Island such transfer was long overdue. I am glad to hear that a new hydrographic survey boat is being provided for in the supplementary estimates, and I do hope that it will be in addition to the Lillooet and not to replace it. That perhaps in some way explains why this vote is smaller than it was last year. It was small enough then, and I am sorry to see it reduced. The members from eastern Canada do not appreciate how urgent is the need for this survey work. I recall a year or two ago that Sir Henry Drayton suggested the cutting down of this vote. That is very easy for an eastern man to say, for such survey work has been carried on in eastern waters for a hundred years, but we on the Pacific coast are only now waking up to the absolute necessity of these hydrographic surveys.
This house will perhaps be interested to know that in many places still our seamen are operating by the aid of charts made by Captain Vancouver when the western Pacific was first discovered, so to speak. Vancouver's charts have proved to be very good so far as they go, but he only did his work at wide intervals. Now, there is a peculiarity in the Pacific coast waters that does not obtain elsewhere to the same extent; that is, there are large numbers of what is known as pinnacle rocks. A pinnacle rock is a small narrow rock which may be only a few yards wide, but it has a point on it that will rip the bottom of a boat just like a knife will cut into cheese. Any general survey is totally inadequate to detect those rocks. To establish their location it is necessary to sweep from point to point. This involves a far more expensive survey than any provided by the old charts made by Captain Vancouver.
I agree with a great deal of what my hon. friend from Skeena has said with regard to the growing necessity of this work, but I am talking now more in the interests of my own district. On the west coast of Vancouver island in the last three years there have been established fishery reduction plants costing between $5,000,000 and $6,000,000, and bringing an enormous return to the general public in the shape of fish meal and fish oil.

It has made a new trade of very great and valuable importance. Necessarily these plants are located in new and untried, so to speak, locations, in remote inlets. Now, the fish oil and fish meal must be taken away as soon as available. A small boat is of no use on that exposed coast. These reduction plants need boats fitted up with tank equipment. They go into one of these uncharted channels and sometimes strike an uncharted rock. The underwriting companies will not allow boats to go into these places on account of the waters being uncharted. That is the necessity, the growing necessity of the work in which this steamer Lillooet is now engaged. To give you some idea of the general benefit of that work I might mention a specific instance. Here is a vote for $495,000. This seems a large sum and there is apparently no return. But the return, though indirect is very great. I know of one place where there was a cannery and the owner chartered a boat to come and take a few thousand cases of salmon. The master, a Norwegian, looked at his chart, saw that the place was not properly charted according to the old chart, and he refused to come in. The result was that it cost the canner a thousand dollars to have I he salmon taken by lighter to a spot where it was considered safe for the steamer to load. A few months after that I got the government to send the Lillooet to chart the place, and at the cost of a few hundred dollars a very valuable service was rendered. That one undertaking alone more than justified the expenditures over a period of months in connection with the Lillooet. I have not a list before me showing the actual work done from year to year by this hydrographic survey, but I can give an idea of the development that is taking place along that line on the west coast. I might quote half a dozen figures showing the increase in the aids to navigation which have been provided in the last eight years. In' 19211 there were eight lighted buoys; to-day there are twenty-four. In 1921 there were one hundred and fifty-two unlighted buoys; to-day there are two hundred and three. In 1921 there were eighty-three lighted beacons; to-day there are one hundred and twenty-four. In 1921 there were thirty-three fog alarms, of which twenty were of the diaphone type-very expensive; to-day, instead of thirty-three, there are forty, twenty-four being diaphones. This gives a vague but significant idea of the development that has taken place in these few years. This work naturally requires a good deal of money to provide expert mechanics, and supplies have to be taken by steamer. : This is taken care of

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
in part by the vote for lighthouse tenders. I am merely trying to convey to the house some idea of the development that has taken place in the last few years, and there is not the slightest suggestion that the Marine department has been too quick to realize our needs; because getting money out of that department is like getting blood out of a stone. There is not much danger of their indulging in waste and extravagance. If they spend a nickle, you may rest assured that they should have spent a dollar. I wish to give them credit if credit is coming to them in that regard, for no man could be more careful of the public purse than the minister of this department. So that if he has put his hand into the treasury to that extent the committee may be assured that it was more than needed. We did particularly need this extra new boat and I am more than pleased to see an estimate to provide for it. I hope it is the intention of the department to keep the Lillooet on as well as the bigger boat, which can do the heavier outside work, the Lillooet being available for necessary operations in more inland waters. I trust the minister will assure me that the Lillooet will be kept in commission as well.
Certainly.

Item agreed to.
Radiotelegraph service and to provide for the construction and maintenance of radiotelegraph ship to shore stations and the general administration of the provisions of the Radio Act and regulations throughout the Dominion, $843,505.

This appropriation is to
provide for the maintenance and operation of government radio stations and for the general administration of radio in 'Canada, including the licensing and inspection of ship stations, private and commercial land stations, broadcasting and receiving stations, and the examination and certification of commercial radio operation. The vote does not include the amount necessary for improving reception.

I presume the minister has
reference to ordinary broadcasting stations. I do not intend to ask any questions in that regard, but I desire some information in reference to government-owned radiotelegraph stations. The government own stations in the east and west and, I believe, on the lake shores as well. I understand that they own radiotelegraph stations which transmit commercial telegrams and also give weather forecasts. In eastern Canada the stations are operated by the Canadian Marconi Company, which I understand is given a subsidy each
year. I wonder why in one case the government deem it necessary to give a subsidy to a private company to operate a system which they own themselves, while in the other case, on the Pacific coast, they operate the government-owned system themselves. Why is it not possible for the government to operate all its systems?

My hon. friend' is correct;
the government own stations on the Pacific and on the Atlantic coast, the system on the Atlantic being operated by the Marconi Company. We are not making any money in the operation of our stations on the Pacific, and I am informed that the Marconi Company is not making money either in the operation of our station in the east.

Is the government losing
money in connection with the Pacific service?
Yes, we are.
What is the loss?

These stations are used
as aids to navigation and the revenue derived from them is far from being sufficient to meet the expenditures.

Is there not some way of
separating the costs of the various services, as between commercial service and the service given to ordinary ships sailing info and out of the ports in British Columbia?

These stations have to be
maintained as aids to navigation and the transmission of commercial messages is only incidental.
Does that apply to the eastern service as well?
Yes, it does.
But why cannot the government operate its own system in the east?

We have a long term contract with the Marconi people, covering a period of eighteen years, which I am informed will expire in 1931. I suggest that it will be opportune then to take into consideration the suggestion made by my hon. friend.

The government have no
control over the men who work in the stations in eastern Canada. These men have to work seven days a week, whereas on the Pacific coast employment conditions are much more satisfactory. Is there anything the government can do to have the eastern men given one day off every week? I do not think I am asking anything out of the way for these employees.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
I am afraid we are not in a position to impose our views on the Marconi Company at present; we can only make representations to them.

In view of the fact that the agreement expires in 1931 and that a new agreement will have to be made, perhaps it might be just as well to take up the question next session, but I have a further matter which comes under this vote. I believe the Department of Marine and Fisheries granted a license to the Marconi Company to operate a beam service from the Pacific coast of this country. I would like to know the terms and conditions of that license.

I might say to my hon.
friend that the Marconi Company has been given a license to operate a beam service from Drummondville, Quebec, to Australia, and also from Drummondville to England. The ordinary fee of $50 was collected for that license. No station has been established on the Pacific coast; the company asked for a license but no station has been erected.

The point is that the
Marconi Company was given a license by the Department of Marine and Fisheries which enabled it to compete with the government-owned Pacific cable system. I want to know from the minister whether, before that license was issued, his department took up the matter with any of the other departments of the government.

This license was not issued during my time as minister, so I am not in a position to give the details, but I should think it would have been submitted to the Post Office Department and other departments interested in the cable. In any case, apparently it was thought that we should not refuse to issue a license which would permit of a very important experiment being carried on. I feel sure that the other' departments interested were consulted.

This is a very important
point. This beam service came into operation within the last few years; it began after I became a member of the house. I do not know exactly how long the minister has been in charge of the department, but I think the beam service between Australia and Canada was established in 1926. I am under the impression that the present minister was in charge of the department in that year, so that I do not think the reason he gave just now is valid. If possible I would like to obtain these particulars from the minister, because I think it is a very important matter when one department issues a license to a

private company which enables that company to compete with a publicly owned utility. In addition to that, so far as I have been able to ascertain we have received no concessions as a result of this service. All other countries which have the advantage of this new system have had their rates lowered by approximately one-third, but no reduction has been made in Canada.
I do not concede that it was necessary to issue this license; I believe the government could have operated the beam system as easily as it operated the cable system, but if the government was determined to issue the license I think it was the duty of the department to secure for this country the concessions which were obtained in other countries. I am afraid the minister is not very well acquainted with the affairs of his department in this regard, but I would like some information as to whether or not the other departments were consulted when the question of issuing this license to a private company was under consideration.
When the bill approving of this cable merger was before the house some time ago the Postmaster General said the license had been granted by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and he had very little information to give the house. I think we should have all the information available on a question of this kind. It may be said that the matter has been disposed of, but in one sense that is not the case, because some time ago the Labour party in Great Britain stated that if they were returned to power they would repudiate this contract between the new corporation and the government. I am rather disappointed that the minister is not able to give us some information on an important question of this kind.

Item agreed to.
Salaries and allowances to light-keepers, $750,000.

Mr. Chairman, I think the
committee should have an explanation of this item, as there is no increase over the vote of last year. A delegation from the light-keepers met the minister and the government some time ago and requested that something be done in the way of granting an increase in salaries. These light-keepers have received no increase in their remuneration for a number of years, and they are the lowest paid officials of the government and do the most hazardous work in the service. I notice there is an item of $25,000 in the supplementary estimates, but I do not know whether or not that is to take care of these increases. If it is, it is a very small amount considering the number of lighthouses and lightships which we have along the coasts of the Atlantic and the Pacific. These men receive a much lower remuneration than is paid to men performing a like service in the United States. This matter has been brought before the house for the last three or four years and representations have been made that a reclassification of these light-keepers should be made by the department and an increase granted, but up to the present time nothing has been done.
I think the minister should take into consideration the representations which have been made to him by different members on both sides of the house, and also the representations which were made to him by the delegation of the light-keepers association, and grant substantial increases to these men. I know of some light-keepers who have to walk from one to three miles at night to light their lights, who cover the same distance in the morning to turn them out and who receive the magnificent sum of $200 per year. Some of these men have not had an increase for twenty years and everyone knows the cost of living has almost doubled in that time. These men are performing a valuable and hazardous service and I submit, Mr. Minister, that the time has arrived when their salaries should be increased. If the minister can increase the salary of his deputy minister and other officials in his department, surely some consideration should be given to these light-keepers who are giving such valuable service to the country.

We have listened to the representations made and we have decided to grant the requests which have been pre-
IMr. Cardin.]
ferred to us. The amount of $25,000 which is provided in the supplementary estimates is to cover increases in salaries of the light-keepers. The lightkeepers were represented by members of their organization, and the amount we are providing in the supplementary estimates is satisfactory to them for the present.

Is the amount sufficient to
cover the increase they ask for?

I understand they were,
as many people do, asking for more than they probably expected to get, but a compromise was reached between them and the department.
On a fifty-fifty basis?
They agreed to that.

This amount of $25,000 is
sufficient to cover the amount agreed upon?
Yes.
It takes in all classes?
No, more particularly the low classes.
Do the ones in the higher class receive any increase?
Not this year.

Is it the intention of the
government to give them an increase next year?

If they press the request,
I am ready to listen to them.
I have no doubt they will.

I may say I expect them
to do so.

Has any arrangement
been made for providing superannuation for lighthouse keepers when they retire from the service? I understand from experience I had with the department in the past, that no superannuation is provided for them because they are classed as part-time employees. This works quite a hardship upon some of the men when they become old in the service. Some provision should be made in regard to superannuation.
Those who are giving only part of their time to the service are not entitled to superannuation but those who are giving their full time are entitled to superannuation, and they receive it.

The question perhaps does not come directly under this item but, as it concerns lighthouses, the minister might

I have not yet received a printed report from Vancouver, but I expect these reports any day.

I understood that a
written report had been received by the department.
A typewritten report.

Yes, but not in printed form.

house to-morrow?

When the delegation of lighthouse keepers waited on the minister last winter, another question was taken up which more particularly concerns the lighthouse keepers of British Columbia and which has not been dealt with to-day. I gather from the officials that they were going to meet the situation, and I should like the assurance of the minister that I am correct in so stating the situation. The question was in connection with annual leave and sick leave. There seemed to be the idea among some of the lighthouse keepers that they had to provide their own substitutes if they went on annual leave and that the same thing applied in connection with sick leave. I understand from the officials-and I would like confirmation from the minister-that the situation is that as regards lighthouse stations that maintain more than one man, arrangements will be made that the head man can take his holiday at a slack time of the year, such as when there is no fog, and leave his deputy in charge. Of course he gets his full pay while he is away. I understand that in the
case of one-man lighthouses the department will get and pay some local man to substitute for him without going to the expense of sending in a man from a distance. As regards sick leave, of course while they cannot give sick leave just for a few days' illness, in the case of a man being seriously ill and having to go away for an operation, the department is willing to provide and pay a substitute to do the work. If that is the situation I would only ask that it be confirmed by the minister, because many men seem to have the idea they are not getting the arrangement that I have suggested.
I am informed that such is the practice.

The minister speaks of the low class. Does that mean those who are temporarily employed on inland waters, for instance, on the great lakes, because their pay is disgraceful? I do not know how they manage to live on it.
The expression "part time" means employees who are giving, for example, one hour or two hours' service a day.
Does this take in the man who is employed on the great lakes for just so many months in the year?
There are on the great lakes a number of men who are what we call full-time employees; they are on the most important lights that we have, but we have others that are only part-time employees.
That is on a shore light where they put in an hour or so a day?
Yes.
What I referred to was a man who goes out on a small island where there is a small light and stays there for four or five months in the summer. Will he benefit by this increase?
I am informed that he will not. The men at the docks are what we call full-time employees.

The man I mean is the one who goes out to a light on an island or on a point of an island and who is there for three, four or five months in the summer. His pay is certainly a pittance. I do not know how he manages to live and feed himself on the amount he receives.

I understand that a certain number of these lightkeepers in the position indicated by my hon. friend from Kingston are also doing other work. Their time is not entirely taken up by looking after the light. They light it when necessary; they take care

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
of it, but they engage in other work. Some of them engage in fishing and other occupations.

Where a returned man has to go periodically to his unit centre for an examination, is it the practice if that period occurs during the time of his employment, to deduct the pay for the two or three days he is absent?
We make no deduction from his salary for that. We arrange to let him go.
Of this appropriation of $25,000, what percentage is to be allowed to the more poorly paid light-keepers throughout the country?
Practically the whole $25,000 goes to the lower paid lightkeepers.
Will this include the part time lightkeepers, some of whom are getting as low as $60 a year?
That is the kind of men I meant.
Yes, they are included.

We have along the Atlantic coast lightkeepers working on full time and receiving four or five hundred dollars a year. What increase are they to get? They are situated in positions where they cannot do anything else, and they must remain there the whole year round.

I am informed that the $25,000 takes care of the class indicated by my bon. friend drawing $400. In regard to the higher class, the suggestion which has been agreed upon is to reconsider their classification. They may be changed from one class to a higher class, and the higher class will, of course, carry a higher salary. That is the idea in regard to the second group of lightkeepers. They may receive their increase through a change in their classification. That is what we propose to do.

For years the lightkeepers on the Atlantic coast, both the full time and the part time men, have not been receiving adequate recompense for their labour. Many of them are placed in practically impossible situations, out on islands where they have no communication with the mainland, and they must remain there the year round. I consider that $25,000 is not adequate to give these men the increased salaries which they should be receiving. This government is expending huge sums of money for other services, and this is one of our very, very important services; it is an aid to navigation. I consider that it is
fMr. Cardin.1
the duty of the government to enable the men they hire to earn a decent livelihood so that they may have the comforts of life that are enjoyed by the people in other communities. I would urge the minister to take seriously into consideration the recommendation of the committee that met him last year and give the lightkeepers not merely this $25,000 but the full amount they asked for.

The higher paid lightkeepers are in grade 1. These men must have assistants in looking after the larger lighthouses. At Cape Race, for instance, the light-keeper has four assistants. At Estevan Point there are also four assistants. The principal lighthouse keeper, drawing $3,060 must support, feed and maintain four other persons. They may not be members of his family. I should just like to be sure about that. Are there any cases where the assistants at these large lighthouses are not members of the principal lighthouse keeper's family?
I am not in a position to say as to that because the lighthouse keeper is not supposed to make a report to us on that point.

I know that in many cases they have to pay out money to assistants who are not members of their family, practically $600 a year. I think that consideration in the way of increased pay should be given to these permanent men who are working in these isolated places, doing wonderful work under very hard conditions. That applies to grades 1, 2 and 3. Consideration also should be given to the part time lightkeepers where the lights have not to be looked after daily. But as regards the permanent lighthouse keepers I do think that if the people of Canada as a whole realized the service these men are performing and the conditions under which they work there would be a real protest at the parsimonious treatment that is being given them in the supplementary estimates. It was only last year that one of these lighthouse keepers situated at a very lonely lighthouse along the British Columbia coast lost his life, foully murdered by some person. It comes as a shock to the community when instances of that kind arise. I am pleased to hear that an annual vacation will be given to the lighthouse keepers and that they will not have to pay out of their own pockets for an assistant to take their place while they are on holiday. Am I correct in that?
Yes, we are doing that.
That is fine.

It is of such vital importance to our patrol system in the waters of British Columbia that I feel sure that when I put a few facts before the committee they will not be merely surprised at conditions there but will receive a decided shock. To-day on the Pacific coast we find the greatest fishery that Canada possesses. That is the only part of Canada at the present time that presents increased fishing problems; these problems are all on on the Pacific seaboard. For instance, we have entered into a halibut treaty for the preservation of that great industry, and we have made a seal industry from which this government obtains annually $100,000. This money goes into the national revenue and is not paid into the fishing department for its development. This bounty is a gift from one of our sea industries. Then lately we have seen the desirability of entering into a salmon treaty for the preservation of that very high class commercial fish, the Sockeye.
What are the facts to-day regarding our fishing? I went to the trouble to get from the bureau of statistics at Washington the report of the tariff investigation that has taken place in the last few weeks in connection with fishing in the United States and in its relation to Canada and other countries. As a preamble to the facts which I am going to give to the committee. I may observe that-the president of the largest fishing establishment in Boston, in giving his evidence before the tariff commission when asking for an increase of 3 cents per pound on processed haddock going in from the Atlantic seaboard into the United States, uttered this sentence, which I am quite convinced will cause every member of this committee to think.
What we want is an equalization basis; having got that, with American brains and American genius, we look after the rest.
To-day in the United States, with a population nearly thirteen times greater than that of Canada, there is a demand thirteen times greater for fish in that market. And here we find this statement in an article:
It has been abundantly proved that the fishing banks to which American fishermen have immediate access are unable to meet the demands of the American market for fish
Fro-m maps compiled by the United States bureau of fisheries indicating the distribution of production, it is made manifest that any further developments in production must be made in waters nearer the Canadian coast than that of the United States.
I will give one more short paragraph which is also illuminating in connection with American inland fisheries; a survey made in American waters proved that they are so depleted that production in these waters is entirely inadequate to meet the demand. Yellow pike, whitefish, yellow perch and jacks, all have suffered depreciation. It is admitted, moreover, by the United States authorities that the production of fresh water fish on the American side of the great lakes is likewise depleted. The blue pike, a highly commercial inland water fish which was obtained in tremendous quantities from American waters up to 1923, has been fished out.
As a preamble to what I am going to say I want to remind hon. members that no phase of this great industry demands the attention of this house and of the people of Canada so much as our Pacific fisheries. What is happening there to-day? Let me go back three years; time and again the Department of Fisheries has been warned that great inroads were being made by American trawlers, and on our fishery grounds only as a last resort on the part of individual Canadian trawlers to undertake to do the police work which the department was unable to do properly because of the lack of an adequate patrol system, with which I will deal in a moment. The smaller boats, except the Malaspina and Givenchy cannot go into these deep waters, swept as they are by terrific storms, and as a result they are unable to give proper service.
The Washington treaty of 1909 undoubtedly has not been lived up to; here is the important section of that treaty, which was; signed at Washington on January 27, 1909:

Surely it is my right, Mr. Chairman, to present to this House of Commons and to this committee the gravity of the situation and the danger threatening this great fishing industry. A grave responsibility rests upon us of preserving and conserving that great industry. I believe the Minister of Maxine and Fisheries knows the complexity and magnitude of this work which he is called upon to perform, but with his double function of Min-
ister of Marine and Fisheries he cannot hope to give the Fisheries department the consideration which it deserves. I would like to quote a few sentences from a very excellent report upon the patrol service and which throws out a hint that this particular service should be improved. The first sentence is:
In view of the immense increase in the number of fishermen and the quantity of fishing gear operated during the year, particularly in the case of salmon, and the resultant keen competition, the difficulties of the patrol service were greatly increased.
And again, and this is much more important:
Several of the present overseer's areas must be considerably reduced.
I will explain the significance of that sentence a little later on. The report continues:
The inspections by guardians and patrolmen are very often unsatisfactory owing to the fact that these officers are usually new men each year.
Those who do not understand the conditions under which these men enter the patrol service cannot get the significance of that sentence. The minister knows that this service is used for patronage purposes. These men see an opportunity of obtaining a job for two or three months and very often some of them have never seen the inside of a boat before.
I know of one instance where a man was placed on one of these patrol boats and I looked up his history and found that he did not know anything about a marine engine.
I do not blame anyone personally, but I blame the system. The system is wrong and wo should have competent men in our patrol system, men who are paid enough to keep them from temptation and bribery. They should be given proper boats and the areas of inspection should be reduced. Moreover, there should be one or two larger boats provided to ply these waters and visit the harbours where hundreds and hundreds of American salmon trawlers are to be found.
It is only since May 11 that any effort has been made to check up this great evil. A recent case was the patrol boat Malaspina which seized five American trawlers and took them to Prince Rupert. They claimed that they came in for shelter, but it was proved by the evidence of the fishery officers in charge of the fisheries that the weather had been fine. They were not in need of water and they had not been forced in through the inclemency of the weather. A few days ago at Zayas island in northern British Columbia another American trawler was seized. The man admitted that he had been fishing, but he was caught redhanded and was forced to make

that admission, and furthermore, he had salmon on board. That boat was a fifteen ton trawler, newly built in Seattle, and had been fishing in Canadian waters. Before I proceed any further, I would like to ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries whether or not Hecate straits are "mare clausum" or considered as being Canadian water.
The department has always claimed that it is.
It is within Canadian waters?
That is our claim but it is not admitted.

I am very glad to hear the minister say that that is our claim. I believe that that is one thing which will have to be fought for as those waters should be considered as being purely Canadian waters. Last year the American trawlers took nearly 2,000,000 pounds of salmon from that area. At the north end of Hecate strait, at the international line, there are hundreds of American traps to be found, and the same condition applies to the southern end of the international line. Then we find hundreds and hundreds of American trawlers plying along our coasts and coming into our harbours and there is no doubt in the world that they are not keeping to the treaty of Washington. If this committee, or this House of Commons, would realize the importance of this matter it would receive immediate attention. The only place in Canada where we have fishing problems is on the Pacific coast. The Atlantic seaboard has been fished for many years and it presents no great problems at the present time. This government should have a Minister of Fisheries who knows these waters and knows the problems surrounding them; that is the only solution of the whole matter.
I do not wish to keep the committee any longer, but I only desire to say that we are wasting time, energy and money unless a constructive policy is adopted. These people should be made to live up to the treaty, a better patrol service should be provided, better conditions of entering that service and conservation of our fish. These should be the important points.

Yes. In answer to the
observations of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Brady), while I have no intention of going into any of the details that he has discussed, referring to his last observation that the proper move would be the appointment of a separate minister to look after the fisheries, I have already said in the house that personally I am not very anxious to continue the office of Minister of Fisheries. What has been stated by my hon. friend relates, if I am not mistaken, to last year.

The results for this year
are very satisfactory. The patrol service has already effected several seizures, and I think the condition has very much improved as compared with what it was last year. At present we have in British Columbia twenty patrol boats. We have two big boats; in district No. 1 we have six smaller ones; in district No. 2, nine, and in district No. 3, five, making a total of twenty. possible with the Northern British Columbia Fishing Association. The department is satisfied that at present the situation has improved, and we hope it will continue to improve.

The minister has given us
the number of patrol boats he has on the Pacific coast. How many has he on the Atlantic? The hon. member for Skeena evidently thinks that we have no fishery problems in the maritime provinces. I should like him to understand that we have quite as many problems and difficulties in the maritime provinces as they have on the Pacific. The minister might also give the number of patrol boats on the great lakes.

We have none on the great lakes, but on the Atlantic coast we have the Arras and the Arleux. We have also the Mildred McColl and the F. P. 1. In New Brunswick we have the Phalarope, the Gannet Rock, in addition to chartered boats. Moreover we are building three boats for the eastern coast of Canada, one to replace the F. P. 1 which has been condemned, a new boat for scallop investigation and1 a new boat for patrol service.

In the first place there are statutory increases and the employment of four new overseers. This includes the travelling expenses and allowances for these officers.
What do the overseers get?

We have two grades, one
receiving from $1,200 to $1,500, and the other from $1,500 to $1,800. This increase also covers special guardians, employment of additional guardians in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Manitoba and Saskatchewan; miscellaneous expenditure, the small amount of $5,000; the building of new boats for the west coast and the east coast, amounting to $137,000. That is the big item in the increase.
How much of that is for the west coast?

$98,000. The existing
wooden boat sheds at Digby island, British Columbia, which were of cheap and fragile construction, are beyond repair and must be replaced at a great cost or deterioration of the boats will be incurred. Additional sheds (Mr. Cardin.]
are now needed, there being no accommodation for some boats. The amount for that is $6,700. We are now providing $20,000 more than last year for air service.

Principally west coast?
Mr. OARiDIN: Altogether west coast.

This patrol service which, I presume, is being operated on the west coast, is rapidly mounting into very large figures. I notice that last year we spent on the patrol service, $228,904, and from the figures given by the minister our expenditure this year will probably be close to $350,000 on the coast. There is a good deal in what the hon. member for Skeena has said. The conditions of which he complains on the west coast of Vancouver island and under which our Canadian fishermen have suffered have prevailed for a long time. We have beyond the west coast of Vancouver island the Swift Shore banks, about twenty-five miles out, and our fishermen should enjoy the advantage of proximity to that bank, but under the old treaty American vessels have the privilege of entering our ports for wood, water, shelter and repairs. I appreciate that it is very difficult for the department to protect our fishermen and prevent what is undoubtedly going on, and that is the use of these numerous harbours on the west coast of Vancouver island as a resting place for the Seattle fleet.
I submit to the minister that we should take soime steps to protect our fishermen on rhe west coast, even to the extent of asking for a modification of that old treaty which is no* longer applicable to present day conditions.
I submit that a great deal of this expenditure-of $350,000 which the government will make-this year is oaused by the fact that we are-endeavouring to protect ourselves against tne misuse of our numerous hafbours on the west coast. I can see the difficulty the department must experience in doing that because to-day it is not unusual to find twenty-five or fifty American boats, which fish off the Swift Shore Banks, resting in our harbours on the west, coast. They can run in and out of these harbours with impunity under this clause in the treaty which permits them to come in for wood, water, shelter and repairs, almost as conveniently as our own fishermen who have their homes on the shore. I submit that the Seattle fleet would be at a great disadvantage, operating two hundred miles away from their base, if they could only use our harbours when there was a real storm on, and then they could come in for safety. I do not think this treaty was ever intended

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
to allow foreign fishermen to come into our harbours and enjoy exactly the same privileges as our own Canadian citizens. The Seattle fleet buy all their supplies in Seattle, and then come up and fish off the Swift Shore banks, enjoy the privileges of our harbours so far as shelter is concerned, and then return to Seattle with their catch, but they are not subject to two cents a pound duty.
I am glad of this opportunity to put these facts before the committee because I think it is a matter that requires the attention of the government, particularly in view of the increased expenditure which is going on from year to year in order to protect ourselves against conditions which it is impossible for us properly to protect ourselves against, regardless of how many boats you put on the patrol service, for there are dozens of harbours, probably forty or fifty, into which these American boats can run, and there is no habitation there at all. It is quite easy for the Seattle fleet in any little blow which would just make the ordinary 'landsmen seasick to run into our harbours and call it a storm, and then immediately go out and fish again when the sun comes out.
How near the shore can they fish, three or twelve miles?

I believe that three miles is the limit, but that is not the real complaint, because I believe that poaching will be done once in a while by all fishermen. It is difficult on a long coast line of 300 miles to prevent poaching altogether, and I do not think there is any serious complaint about that. What we complain about is that common use of our harbours by foreign fishermen, and our own people.

I would like to endorse
everything that the hon. member for Vancouver North has said. He has outlined the situation as it exists. What the remedy is I do not know unless it be greater vigilance on our part. Some years ago it was the practice never to interfere with these men at ail. There seemed to be some doubt about the correct interpretation of the treaty, and I had a good deal to do with pressing the department to take the matter up. Two years ago the department finally decided to take action, and in order not to be too harsh at first they first of all warned these men, and then on the second offence they seized the vessel. I think last year five or six boats were seized. The United States government took the attitude that we were all wrong, that we had not interpreted the treaty correctly. I believe the matter never went to the courts. The boats
were confiscated or released on paying a very heavy fine. I saw in the local papers only a few weeks ago that quite a number of them had been taken recently, some in the constituency of my hon. friend from Skeena, and some in the district I represent. I can only suggest that the government should be more vigilant in this matter and make an example of these foreign fishermen and vessels when they catch them.

The difficulty the government experiences is in connection with this clause in the old treaty which gives foreign vessels the right to come in for wood, water, shelter and repairs, and until that treaty is modified all we can expect is that the government do the best they can, but they will not get very far in protecting the interests of our fishermen in these harbours because you can readily see that a man could shutoff his gasoline engine or put it out of business and then come into port and say he wants to fix the engine up. Many a man has said that when he has been approached-"I am fixing up my engine"-and he is allowed in under that clause in the treaty which enables him to come in to make repairs. I really think that in the interests of our fishermen the treaty should be revised. It has been in effect for one hundred years, and I think it would be a good thing to bring it up to date.

Item agreed to.
Building fishways and clearing rivers, $20,000.

It is not very often that this side of the house criticizes the government for not spending enough money, but this vote for clearing streams is absurd; it is totally inadequate, and in some cases the money has not even been used. It requires no expert in fishing to know that you must remove obstructions from rivers and streams if fish are unable to get up those rivers and streams; and on our coast there are dozens of streams in which improvements of this kind could be made to great advantage. I should like to see the vote sufficiently large so that if applications came in to the department, and investigation warranted it, a proper expenditure could be made to improve any stream where necessary. I know of one steam at least which would require the whole of this vote to put it into proper condition. The expenditure would be worth while, and as a business proposition it would be made. But the department has always been handicapped by the limitation of this particular vote.
Last year we spent practically the amount voted-$19,000. I agree with my hon. friend that more work should be undertaken.
The vote should be $100,000, and even if you did not use it all you would at least have the money on hand to do work which is of primary importance.

I agree with the hon. member that this vote is a mere pittance compared to what it should be to take care of so important a matter as the clearing of streams. We have the same difficulty in Nova Scotia. In some of our rivers, which were splendid salmon rivers, this fish is now almost extinct; the salmon are unable to get up the rivers on account of obstructions. I wish to read an editorial that appeared in the Halifax Herald two or three days ago, bearing on this subject:
Protect The Salmon
There is urgent need for moTe adequate protection in relation to the salmon streams of Nova Scotia. If this adequate protection is not afforded, these fine fish will cease to exist in streams now famous as anglers' haunts.
On certain streams facilities are provided for the passage of salmon upstream, but when the small fish come down they get into the flume and are destroyed.
What is needed, The Herald is advised, is a screen on the flume to keep the small fish out.
This matter is giving concern to those interested in conservation of the fish of the province, and it should receive immediate and effective attention.
I 'believe this matter was brought to the attention of the minister last year by the senior member for Halifax, and it is one that should receive the immediate consideration of the department. Our rivers and streams should be so cleared as to enable salmon to get up and down. This means a great deal to the province of Nova Scotia and to every province in the Dominion. If there is not sufficient money in the vote for the purpose, it would be advisable for the minister to ask for a further appropriation.

Last year I called the minister's attention to this very item. There is not much use clearing rivers if you do not take precautions to see that fishways are maintained. The preservation of spawning beds is a most important thing. As I pointed out to the minister, charters are being granted to power companies for the erection of power sites on rivers which are navigable and which should come under the jurisdiction of the federal department. If this matter does not come within the scope of the federal department, then I submit that there should be a certain amount of cooperation with the provincial governments to see that fishways are made on these rivers. I have been over a great number of them and I cannot find one. Consequently, both by damming and by the

erection of power sites, the old spawning grounds are being destroyed, and the future supply of fish is endangered. It is more important to preserve fishways and spawning grounds than it is to maintain hatcheries in an attempt to restore the fish. We took this matter up
last year with the Ontario government, but my hon. friend understands the difficulties that have to be met. No money spent in

What is this for?

This appropriation is to
encourage the production, to extend the demand and to improve marketing facilities. With a view to having the growing demands for fresh fish supplied as far as possible by our inshore fishermen, an experiment was [Mr. A. E. Ross.)
started last year in the collection of fish along the coast, where those supplying the fresh fish markets would agree to buy all the fish caught. The portion of the coast covered was from Port Bickerton, Guysborough county, to Canso. The Maritime Fish Corporation, particularly, entered enthusiastically into the experiment. The experiment was successful and resulted in the building of several new boats by the fishermen and in other preparations being made for more intensive fishing. It was continued there last season, when over one million pounds more cod and haddock were transported than in 1927. Another result is that during the present winter at least twenty-two new boats are being built by tihe fishermen, wharves are being enlarged and additional ice and bait facilities are being provided.
The experiment was extended last summer to tihe portion of the southeast coast of Cape Breton from Main a Dieu to Canso, where again the Maritime Fish Corporation understock to buy the fish; to the portion of the cost from Sonora, Guysborough county, to Halifax, along which the National Fish Company of Halifax and Messrs Mitchell and McNeil undertook to buy, and along the portion of the coast from Cape Negro to Lockeport and Shelburne. The idea is to collect the fish from places where it is not easy to market them and take them to where they can be marketed advantageously.

That would seem to apply
to the development of the industry; how about the conservation?
I think the word "conservation" does not apply to the fish but to the fishing industry.

There is one point I would
like to mention in this connection; I refer to the question of our deep sea fishing off the west coast of Vancouver island. I would like to ask if any representations have been received from the fishery interest on the Columbia river with regard to the restriction or the regulation of the fishing season off that coast?

I suppose my hon. friend
refers to spring salmon?
Yes.
Representations have been made but we are not yet in a position to state whether or not those representations are correct.

I think I might add that it is contended by our fishermen that it is not true that later on the fish are bigger; they claim that they can occasionally catch immature fish o2 the west coast of Vancouver island and, as the hon. member for North Vancouver has truly said, they violently resent the idea that they should be restricted in any way for the benefit of the Columbia river fishermen. I drew this matter to the attention of the government a couple of years ago in a similar endeavour to take time by the forelock, as my hon. friend has said.

For the benefit of the committee I might say that the biological society, if my memory serves me correctly, by tagging a great many fish on the Swift Shore banks, showed that when the fish were not interfered with 70 per cent found their way to the Columbia river, and all but a small percentage of the remainder went to Puget Sound. Only a very small proportion reached the Fraser river, so that of the entire catch on the Swift Shore banks, if those fish were not caught, probably not over 10 per cent at the most would find their way into Canadian waters. So it will be easy to understand the deep concern which is felt by our neighbours in desiring to conserve these fish for themselves at our expense.

This item has been in the
estimates year after year, and has remained at the figure'of $130,000; I think last year was the first time the full amount was expended. The item was originally included in the estimates for the purpose of assisting in the conservation and development of the deep sea fisheries and also to create a demand for fish, but within the last year or two I do not think one dollar has been spent in an e2ort to create that demand. I commend the minister for the action he has taken in having a number of boats collect the fish from the outlying districts of the maritime provinces and take them to the central markets. That has been a splendid thing for the fishermen but it has not created a demand for the fish after they are landed.
I find on looking up the accounts that of the $130,000 voted last year $66,000 was expended in connection with the commission which was appointed to investigate the fisheries. Surely that should not be put under the head of fish conservation. I find also that $17,000 was expended for the extermination of hair seals. Last year we passed an item of $25,000 for that purpose, but we find that a part of this $130,000 has been used to pay bounties in that connection. I just want to show the inefficiency of this department and its inability to cope with the problems of an industry which is of so much importance to this country and which, if properly looked after, would provide for all time sea food in much greater quantities than it is available to-day. I wonder if hon. members aTe aware of the fact that in the maritime provinces we have not increased our fish production since 1910; the figures for that year and for 1927 are almost the same. In 1928 there was a slight increase in the value but none in the amount of the catch, which goes to show that there must be some great inefficiency in this department. I am bringing this matter to the attention of the committee because this item has appeared in the estimates year after year. It was intended for the purpose of increasing the consumption of fish in this country, but the department has not been able to expend it until last year, and they would not have expended it last year had it not been for the royal commission, which took up a large portion of that $130,000. I think the minister should try to create a further demand for our fish as we could sell double the quantity of fish in this country if we had some assistance by way of advertising and had a good live department which would look after the industry as it should be looked after. We have been drifting along for the last twenty years and I hope the attempted
